claims.text: A reader who wants one deck from SlideShare is offered a 30-day trial and then £10.99 a month, with no one-off option unless the author switched one on.
claims.quote: offered a 30-day trial and then £10.99 a month

value.unit: GBP a month after a 30-day trial

claims.text: The uploader agreement of August 2024 says it does not entitle the author to any payment, royalties, remuneration or other compensation.
claims.quote: does not entitle You to any payment, royalties, remuneration, or other compensation

claims.text: The same agreement grants a royalty-free, sublicensable licence to monetise, charge for, restrict access to and train machine learning and large language models on the work.
claims.quote: train machine learning, large language, or other statistical or data models

claims.text: The general terms forbid users from training large language models on the same content: the right the platform reserves for itself it withholds from its users.
claims.quote: The right the platform reserves for itself it withholds from its users.

claims.text: The owner is a party to this, with 69 presentations on SlideShare uploaded over fifteen years, downloadable because he switched the setting on.
claims.quote: I have 69 presentations on SlideShare, uploaded since the platform's early years

claims.text: SlideShare was founded in October 2006, LinkedIn bought it in May 2012 for about $119 million, Microsoft bought LinkedIn in 2016, and Scribd acquired SlideShare in 2020.
claims.quote: LinkedIn bought it in May 2012 for about $119 million.

claims.text: When the paywall arrived in September 2021 authors found an account-level checkbox allowing download without a subscription, which one writer reported as off by default.
claims.quote: which one writer who documented it in October 2021 reported as off by default

claims.text: Scribd's 2026 corporate site describes SlideShare as twenty-five million presentations, fifteen million fewer than the forty million cited at the sale, without public explanation.
claims.quote: describes SlideShare as twenty-five million presentations, which is fifteen million fewer than the number cited at the sale

claims.text: About forty million visits a month still arrive at slideshare.net, most from search, which is why nothing has replaced it.
claims.quote: about forty million visits a month still arrive, most from search

claims.text: Fifteen years of embeds, backlinks and search ranking are inertia in Wardley's sense, and a stronger moat than the technology.
claims.quote: Simon Wardley's observation is the right one: "Past success breeds inertia."

claims.text: The complaint is easy to overstate: the uploader keeps copyright, the licence is non-exclusive, and the owner uploaded most decks under a Creative Commons licence.
claims.quote: The uploader keeps copyright. The licence is non-exclusive.

claims.text: The three complaints, a subscription sold for one file, no say and no share, and not knowing where the work went, are all allowed by the licence; the service an author would choose does not exist.
claims.quote: The licence allows all three, which is why the complaint is not that anyone broke a rule.

claims.text: An author can send a right-of-access request under GDPR Article 15 asking the ordinary things and two unusual ones: view and download counts per upload, and the recipients of any licensing.
claims.quote: asking the ordinary things and two unusual ones

claims.text: The European Data Protection Board's guidelines say the right of access includes inferred and derived data, including personal data created by a service provider.
claims.quote: includes both inferred and derived data, including personal data created by a service provider

claims.text: The Court of Justice ruled in January 2023 that a controller must name the actual recipients of personal data where it can, not only categories.
claims.quote: The Court of Justice ruled in January 2023 that a controller must name the actual recipients where it can, not only categories.

claims.text: Article 19 of the 2019 Copyright Directive gives authors a yearly right to comprehensive information on the exploitation of their works, including all revenues generated.
claims.quote: up to date, relevant and comprehensive information on the exploitation of their works

claims.text: Whether a royalty-free upload licence falls within the transparency duty is untested, and the UK said in January 2020 it would not implement the Directive.
claims.quote: The UK said in January 2020 it would not implement the Directive

claims.text: The owner will send the right-of-access request for his own 69 decks, and the answer goes in the first article the ledger is built for.
claims.quote: I will send the request for my own 69 decks

claims.text: Every author gets an encrypted, versioned vault that nobody without a key can read, including the host; a service that cannot read the content cannot sell it or change the terms.
claims.quote: Every author gets a vault.

claims.text: Keys decide access rather than settings: a setting lives on a server and changes with its owner, a key lives with the author and is verified by anyone.
claims.quote: A setting lives on a server and changes when the server's owner changes. A key lives with the author and is verified by anyone.

claims.text: Decryption happens in the reader's browser; the one bounded exception is an attested enclave that handles one deck's plaintext in memory for one request.
claims.quote: The one bounded exception is the unlock service, an attested enclave that handles one deck's plaintext in memory for one request

claims.text: Seven roles, storage host, key service, unlock service, payments, identity, the front and add-ons, are separated so no party holds more than one of the content, the keys and the money.
claims.quote: The plan separates the roles so that no party holds more than one of the content, the keys and the money

claims.text: To pay once and download, the reader sees the author's price with the author's 85% and the platform's 15%; a receipt becomes a ten-minute key and the ledger line goes to the author's vault.
claims.quote: The reader presses Download original and sees the price the author set, the author's 85% and the platform's 15%.

value.unit: percent of a one-off payment to the author

claims.text: A private grant can be revoked, but a file already downloaded is the reader's, and the plan says so on every grant rather than pretending otherwise.
claims.quote: A file already downloaded is the reader's, and the plan says so on every grant rather than pretending otherwise.

claims.text: The owner's shelf is 69 decks of about 5 MB each, 345 MB in all, and serving it for a month costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download.
claims.quote: 69 decks, about 5 MB each, 345 MB in all

claims.text: A UK card through a mainstream processor costs 1.5% plus 20p with a 30p minimum, so a £1 download loses about a fifth of its price to the rail.
claims.quote: A UK card through a mainstream processor costs 1.5% plus 20p with a 30p minimum

value.unit: percent plus 20p, 30p minimum, per card payment

claims.text: The platform pays the card fee out of its 15%; its margin is in wallet top-ups, batched settlements and add-ons at a 70% author share, not in the author's share.
claims.quote: The platform's margin is in wallet top-ups, where one card fee covers several downloads, in batching settlements, and in add-ons at a 70% author share

claims.text: The plan's first open question is which payment rail a UK or EU front can offer a person at under five pence a transaction.
claims.quote: the plan's first open question is which rail a UK or EU front can offer a person at under five pence a transaction

claims.text: What the service sells is provenance: assurance that this file, with this hash, was published by this person, who is who they say they are.
claims.quote: Strip the storage and payments away and what remains is the thing a reader cannot get anywhere else

claims.text: The plan is published as the Deck Vault with a read key: ten plan documents, the access letter, a register of ten risks as acceptances, and a working mock.
claims.quote: a register of ten risks written as acceptances with a holder and a date

claims.text: Nothing in the build order beyond the vault exists: no unlock enclave, no receipt that becomes a key, no front from a read key alone, no migration tool, and no rail under five pence.
claims.quote: Nothing in the build order beyond the vault exists.

claims.text: The owner will build step zero, one author's shelf as a vault with per-deck read keys and an embed per deck, for his own decks.
claims.quote: I will build step zero for my own decks, because I want a home for them that I hold the keys to.

claims.text: The facts about SlideShare and Scribd are from their own help pages, terms and dated press reports; the UK price is the owner's observation.
claims.quote: where a number could only be observed, the UK price for one, it is marked as my observation

claims.text: Whether the right to train models on uploads has been exercised could not be found out; no public report of a licensing deal turned up.
claims.quote: Whether the right has been exercised, I could not find out
